newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Zhu calls on state firms to slash payrolls.
newsitem.headline: China's Zhu calls on state firms to slash payrolls.

text.p: Chinese economic tsar Zhu Rongji has called on ailing state firms to slash their payrolls to boost efficiency, pledging Beijing would refine bankruptcy rules for the sector, the Xinhua news agency said,
Central authorities would standardise bankruptcy procedures and encourage more mergers while loss-making state firms were expected to reduce redundant staff, Xinhua on Friday quoted Zhu as saying.
"Increasing economic restructuring, speeding up the pace of change in state firms and pushing mergers, bankruptcy and re-employment programmes for these enterprises are all necessary," Zhu said.
Cities that had been chosen to handle bankruptcies should set up special working groups to handle the closures, mergers and re-employment plans, Zhu said.
"The pilot cities will have to draft plans for mergers and bankruptcies and must report to the upper authorities and localities must set up re-employment centres at all levels," he said.
Local officials should explain the bankruptcy programmes to laid-off workers to help them understand that such closures were in their long-term interests, Zhu said.
Enterprises that merged with ailing state firms would enjoy exemptions on loan interest and other preferential policies, Zhu said.
Beijing's communist rulers have been trying to promote the use of mergers rather than bankruptcies to liquidate firms that have no hope of getting out of the red.
The government had set aside a maximum of 30 billion yuan ($3.6 billion) of reserve funds in state banks to deal with losses resulting from bankruptcies this year, Zhu said.
Beijing would standardise bankruptcy procedures to try to prevent false bankruptcies and evasion of debt, Zhu said.
Bankrupt factories were expected to close their doors and dismiss all staff, he said, adding that money from the sale of assets of bankrupt firms should be used to find jobs for former workers.
People laid off from state firms should be paid stipends to cover their daily needs and should be given assistance in finding new jobs, he said.
Those businesses unable to make such payments would be given special subsidised bank loans by local governments and access to insurance and relief funds, he said.
Beijing has been reluctant to push ahead with bankruptcies, fearing that mass unemployment from too many closures will cause social unrest.
The number of bankruptcies in China rose to 6,232 in 1996, up by more than 160 percent from the year before, and analysts have said the figure for this year could soar to more than 10,000.
